Plus, Anthropic’s slide continues
 

Anthropic’s IPO has turned into a bust. Its shares slipped below the offering price on Tuesday and appear to be headed for more losses today. The slide is poisoning the well for companies still hoping to raise money from a public that’s growing less optimistic about the earning power of artificial intelligence, including OpenAI. Futures point to sharp losses for U.S. stocks overall before Thanksgiving with tech names set to be hit hardest. Markets A.M. will be taking a holiday break and returning to your inboxes on Monday.

Bah, humbug

 

“Black Friday” can mean two very different things depending on the context—a terrible day for stocks or a great one for shoppers.

 

This week will probably only see the latter version. As usual, it’ll be studied as a barometer of American consumers’ health. High pump prices, rising interest rates and low sentiment notwithstanding, predictions of a decent holiday shopping season from the likes of the National Retail Federation should hold up.

 

Even more gut-wrenching stock-market selloffs like last Friday’s won’t change that because holiday spending plans are fairly locked-in. The two aren’t completely unconnected, but it’s complicated. Retailers feared silent cash registers back in 1987 after that October’s record crash and were pleasantly surprised.

 

At the time of the 1987 crash, though, stocks made up just 15% of Americans’ financial assets. That marked a more than 10-year high. Today it’s above 48%, which far exceeds even the peak of the dot-com bubble.

 

A lot of that stock is owned by the out-of-sight rich, of course. Elon Musk won’t be skimping on gifts for his at least 14 children because SpaceX shares tumbled.

 

But merely well-off Americans, those between the 80th and 98th percentiles of wealth, check their 401(k) balances a lot more often. Their household net worth ranges between about $1 million and $10 million.

 

Back in the mid-1980s, overall spending by households in the top quintile was around three times as much as the lowest quintile. Today that’s more than four times. Recent anecdotes from retailers, hotel chains and airlines indicate that the mass-affluent have become even more important customers as poorer cohorts pull back.

 

Economists know that some decisions to spend are based on how rich people feel, not how much they earn. Oxford Economics estimates that a one dollar change in financial wealth results in a nearly 4 cent change in spending nationally.

 

Increasingly, that wealth is made up of stocks tied directly or indirectly to AI, which reached some 40% of the S&P 500’s value this summer. Even if the data-center boom underpinning a chunk of U.S. economic growth doesn’t suffer, consumer spending could if confidence in what kind of returns those investments will produce takes a hit.

 

Optimism over the AI boom is one reason why anemic consumer-confidence surveys have been so out of sync with overall spending, writes labor economist Gad Levanon, chief economist of the Burning Glass Institute. Those surveys poll everyone. But a bump to the spending of an affluent household emboldened by a jump in their stock-market wealth outweighs a slight pullback by a lower-income household.

 

This month’s choppiness in AI stock values arrived too late to ruin Christmas. More of the same could make next year less merry.

↘️SoftBank Group: The Japanese tech investment group is also under the microscope of credit-conscious investors. Shares fell to their lowest level in more than a year in Tokyo.

 

↘️Dell Technologies: The company lifted its guidance and said revenue doubled for the third quarter. Still, shares were more than 7% lower premarket.

 

↘️Workday: Above-expectation revenue in the third quarter wasn’t enough to stop shares in the human resources group falling by more than 10% premarket.
